description: Vitals is an intelligent health monitoring software designed to monitor astronauts' physical well-being during space missions. It tracks essential health parameters such as heart rate, blood oxygen levels, body temperature, sleep patterns, and physical activity. The system analyses health data to identify unusual changes, detect potential risks, and generate early alerts. It also provides personalised health insights to help astronauts maintain their well-being in challenging space environments.
summary: VITALS is offline-first health-monitoring software built for astronauts on long-duration missions, where help from Earth can be minutes to tens of minutes away. A hand-built ESP32 sensor box reads heart rate and SpO₂ from a MAX30102 pulse oximeter, a real or simulated ECG, and cabin temperature, humidity, and air quality, sent over USB, Bluetooth, or Wi-Fi to a crew dashboard that marks every vital green, yellow, or red against medically grounded ranges and the crew member’s own baseline. Seven subject-focused chatbots answer first-aid and space-health questions from a knowledge library sourced from NASA and partner-agency research; genuine emergencies are always handled by built-in first-aid logic, never an AI model, and each chatbot reads its answers aloud in its own voice. A 3D training simulator puts the crew through seven scenarios — dehydration, CO₂ buildup, sleep loss, a radiation storm, a spacewalk repair — where choices carry consequences into later missions. Every page, 3D model, voice line, and knowledge article is cached for full offline use: a signed-in crew member stays signed in with no connection, and every reading, profile edit, and status update syncs to the database the moment the link returns — even after the mission ends.
details:
What it does: VITALS has four parts: a sensor box placed in the crew’s module; a readings dashboard that classifies heart rate, SpO2, ECG, room temperature, and humidity against safe ranges and the crew member’s own baseline; a set of seven chatbots (one per health topic — fluid shift, bone and muscle, hygiene, isolation, medicine, environment, and a general health assistant) that answer questions and give first-aid steps; and a 3D training simulator with seven voice-acted mission scenarios.

The hardware: A hand-built sensor box, centered on an ESP32 microcontroller. It reads heart rate and blood oxygen from a MAX30102 pulse oximeter, a real ECG trace from an AD8232 sensor, cabin temperature and humidity from a DHT11 sensor, and air quality from an MQ-135 gas sensor. Two OLED screens on the box show live readings to the crew and the cabin conditions. It sends one JSON reading a second over USB serial, and can also be reached wirelessly over Bluetooth or a local Wi-Fi link, so the website works the same way whichever one is used.

How it works: The sensor box streams live readings over USB serial, Bluetooth, or a local Wi-Fi WebSocket link. The web app runs as an installable, offline-first progressive web app: a service worker caches every page, 3D model, and audio file after one online visit, so the whole site — chatbots, simulator, and readings — keeps working with no connection at all, for the length of a mission, once you’ve signed in at least once. Chatbot answers come first from a curated library of space-health facts drawn from NASA and partner-agency sources; for emergencies, the system always uses built-in first-aid rules rather than any AI model, so critical advice never depends on a generative model’s judgment. When online, an optional cloud language model (Cloudflare Workers AI) and, locally, an on-device model (Ollama) rephrase library answers into a more natural conversation, with every reply checked against the source facts before it’s shown, so the assistant can’t invent treatment advice. Each chatbot has its own voice and reads its answers aloud on request. Readings, crew profile edits, and baseline changes made offline are queued on the device and uploaded automatically, in batches, the moment the connection returns — which could be after the whole mission, since a signed-in crew member’s session is kept through long offline stretches rather than expiring and locking them out.

How to use it: A crew member signs up or signs in once — this step needs an internet connection, as does signing out later — and fills in their crew card: name, role, crew ID, and personal baselines like resting heart rate and sleep. On the Live Monitor page they pair their sensor over USB, Bluetooth, or Wi-Fi, or use the built-in Demo mode to try VITALS with no hardware at all. From there, readings update live on the dashboard and each health module page (Bone & Muscle, Fluid Shift, Environment, Hygiene, Isolation, Medicine), each one marked green, yellow, or red. Anyone can type a symptom or question to the relevant chatbot and turn on “Read aloud” to hear the answer spoken back. The Simulator lets the crew train through any of the seven scenarios in any order, with their choices affecting later quests and a final scored debrief. Commanders and flight surgeons get a crew-wide status board on the account page. Once signed in, everything else — chatbots, simulator, readings, the account page — keeps working offline for as long as needed.

Benefits and impact: Long-duration missions put much of the responsibility for spotting health changes on the astronauts themselves, with no doctor on board and communication delays that make real-time guidance from Earth impractical. VITALS gives the crew an always-available first read on their own condition and a trained way to practice handling emergencies before they happen for real, without needing a live connection to function.

Tools and technologies: React, TypeScript, and three.js for the web app and 3D scenes; an ESP32 (Arduino framework) sensor box with a MAX30102 pulse oximeter, AD8232 ECG front end, DHT11 and MQ-135 environmental sensors, and OLED displays, connected over USB, Bluetooth, or Wi-Fi; Supabase (Postgres with row-level security) for accounts and cross-device sync; Cloudflare Workers AI and a locally run Ollama model for the online/offline chatbot brains; browser-native text-to-speech for live chatbot voices; Kokoro-generated recorded voice lines for the simulator’s crew and mission control.

AI tool use: Claude (Anthropic) was used throughout development to write and review code, draft the chatbot knowledge library and prompts, help design the UI, and help draft the documentation and presentation text, under the team’s direction; the team reviewed and edited all content, including the safety logic and the final slides. The VITALS chatbots run on Google’s open Gemma models: Gemma 4 (26B) through Cloudflare Workers AI when online, and Gemma 3 270M locally through Ollama when offline; they support decisions only and never diagnose. The simulator’s spoken voice lines were generated with Kokoro, an open-source AI text-to-speech model, run locally and recorded as audio files. No images or video in the final project are SI-generated: the presentation uses screenshots of our website and our own photos, the website uses real photography and NASA 3D Resources models, and no SI-generated content uses NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.
